title: 11. Observability & SRE: Metrics
summary: Metrics are numeric measurements of system behavior sampled at intervals and stored as time series, enabling cheap aggregation, fast alerting, and long-term trend analysis without preserving individual events.
objectives: Explain the four metric types: counter, gauge, histogram, summary. When would you use each?
What is metric cardinality, and why does it cause "cardinality explosion"?
Compare pull-based (Prometheus) and push-based (StatsD) metrics collection.
What are the RED and USE frameworks, and how do they complement each other?

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Metrics are numeric measurements of system behavior sampled at intervals and stored as time series, enabling cheap aggregation, fast alerting, and long-term trend analysis without preserving individual events.
A metric is a single number attached to a timestamp and a small set of labels, recorded at regular intervals. Where a log line tells you "this request failed at 03:14 with code 502," a metric tells you "the 502 rate is now 4% of all requests, up from 0.1% an hour ago." The metric loses the identity of the individual request but gains the ability to aggregate across millions of requests into a single time series that costs a few bytes per data point. This trade-off — detail for aggregatability — is the foundation of operational monitoring. Netflix's Atlas system, which replaced a patchwork of per-team Graphite installations in 2014, stores roughly 2 billion unique time series and answers queries across years of history in under a second, a feat possible only because metrics compress and aggregate so aggressively. Metrics are the cheapest way to know what is happening to a system at scale.

The four canonical metric types are counter, gauge, histogram, and summary. A counter is a monotonically increasing number that resets only on process restart — total requests served, total bytes sent, total errors. Counters measure rates; you almost always apply a `rate()` function over a window to convert them into per-second values. A gauge is a number that can go up or down — current memory usage, active connections, queue depth, CPU utilization. Gauges measure instantaneous state. A histogram samples observations into configurable buckets and stores a count per bucket plus a sum and total count, allowing you to compute percentiles (p50, p95, p99) at query time. Histograms are essential for latency tracking because averages hide tail behavior. A summary is similar to a histogram but computes percentiles client-side and stores them directly; it is more expensive on the client and cannot aggregate percentiles across instances correctly (you cannot average p99s), so histograms are almost always preferred in modern systems. Prometheus, the de facto open-source standard since 2016, ships with all four types and added Native Histograms in 2023 to address the bucket-cardinality problem.

Labels are key-value pairs attached to a metric — `http_requests_total{method="GET", route="/api/orders", status="200"}`. Labels let you slice the same metric by any dimension at query time without emitting separate metrics. They are enormously powerful and enormously dangerous. The cardinality of a metric series is the product of distinct values across all its labels; a metric with labels for `user_id` and `session_id` and `request_id` can produce unbounded series that explode memory in the metrics backend. The canonical horror story is an e-commerce team whose Datadog bill went from $40K to $1.2M in one month because a debug log was parsed into a metric with a per-session UUID label, creating hundreds of millions of distinct series. The rule of thumb, enforced by code review at every mature observability team, is: never put high-cardinality values (user IDs, session IDs, request IDs, full URLs) into metric labels — those belong in logs and traces. Labels should have cardinality in the tens or low hundreds; if a label has more than ~100 distinct values, it is almost certainly wrong.

The two dominant collection models are pull (Prometheus) and push (StatsD, Datadog Agent). In pull, the metrics backend scrapes each service's `/metrics` HTTP endpoint on a fixed interval (typically 15–60 seconds); the service exposes its current counter and gauge values, and the backend records them. Pull is operationally simple because services do not need to know where the backend is, and the backend automatically detects when a service disappears (a failed scrape is itself a useful signal). Push requires each service to actively send metrics to a collector; this is necessary when services sit behind firewalls or run as ephemeral jobs (AWS Lambda, batch workers) that exit before the next scrape. StatsD, originally built at Etsy in 2011 and still ubiquitous, uses UDP push because UDP fire-and-forget was simpler than TCP in the era of pre-container infrastructure. Modern systems often hybridize: services expose Prometheus-style `/metrics` for long-lived processes and use the Prometheus push gateway for ephemeral jobs, with a single backend pulling from both.

The two most influential metric frameworks are RED and USE, both codified at Netflix. RED (Rate, Errors, Duration) is for request-driven services: every service should expose the request rate, the error rate, and the latency distribution, all broken down by route. USE (Utilization, Saturation, Errors) is for resources: every resource — CPU, disk, network, queue — should be measured for utilization (how busy), saturation (how queued), and errors (how many failed). Together they form a checklist that ensures no critical dimension is unmonitored. Google's SRE book added the Four Golden Signals (Latency, Traffic, Errors, Saturation) which is essentially RED plus USE-style saturation, and is now the most cited framework in SRE job descriptions. A service without RED metrics is effectively unmonitored, no matter how many ad-hoc gauges it emits.

The real-world example is Uber's M3, which replaced their StatsD + Graphite stack in 2017. Uber's scale (over 4,000 microservices, billions of rides per year) made StatsD's per-metric network overhead prohibitive and Graphite's storage engine unable to keep up. M3, designed as a distributed metrics platform, natively supports multi-cluster aggregation, native histograms, and a query language (M3QL) that compiles to a columnar execution engine. Uber reported a 60x reduction in metrics infrastructure cost compared to the equivalent Graphite deployment and now stores over 6.6 billion time series. The lesson is that at extreme scale, the metric backend itself becomes a distributed systems problem, and the choice of backend shapes what queries are even possible — Graphite's storage made multi-year queries painful, M3 made them fast, Prometheus alone struggles at Uber scale without federation.

The trade-off in metrics design is precision versus cost. Every additional label, every finer bucket boundary, every shorter scrape interval costs storage and query time. A well-designed metrics stack consciously limits what it collects: low-cardinality labels, histogram buckets chosen to span the interesting latency range (1ms, 5ms, 10ms, 50ms, 100ms, 500ms, 1s, 5s, 10s), scrape intervals of 15–60 seconds. The Pareto rule applies: 5% of metrics deliver 95% of operational value, and the rest are speculative or forgotten. Periodic metric audits — tagging every metric with an owner and a "last queried" timestamp, then deleting unused ones — are as important as adding new ones.

sections.body:
### Mermaid Diagram
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[App: counter/gauge/histogram] -->|expose /metrics| B[Prometheus scrape]
    B -->|pull every 15s| C[(TSDB storage)]
    C --> D[Grafana dashboard]
    C --> E[Alertmanager]
    A -.->|alternative push| F[StatsD / Datadog Agent]
    F -->|push UDP/TCP| G[(Backend)]
    G --> D
```

### ASCII Diagram
```
+-----------+   expose /metrics    +-------------+
|  Service  | -------------------- | Prometheus  |
| counter   |   text exposition    |   server    |
| gauge     |   format             +-------------+
| histogram |                            |
+-----------+                            | scrape 15s
                                         v
                                 +----------------+
                                 |  TSDB storage  |
                                 |  (compressed   |
                                 |   blocks)      |
                                 +----------------+
                                  |          |
                       query     |          | alert
                                  v          v
                              +------+  +----------+
                              |Grfan.|  |AlertMgr  |
                              +------+  +----------+
```

### Walkthrough
1. The service increments counters and updates gauges in memory using a client library (prometheus_client, micrometer).
2. The library exposes a `/metrics` endpoint in Prometheus text exposition format, listing each metric with its labels and current value.
3. The Prometheus server scrapes the endpoint every 15–60 seconds, appends the samples to its TSDB (compressed on-disk blocks), and evaluates alert rules against the stored series.
4. Grafana queries the TSDB to render dashboards; Alertmanager fires when rules breach thresholds.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
```python
# metrics_mock.py - runnable; simulates counter/gauge/histogram with simple aggregation
import random, time, threading
from collections import defaultdict

class Counter:
    """Monotonic; only reset on restart."""
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name, self.value = name, 0
        self.lock = threading.Lock()
    def inc(self, n=1, **labels):
        with self.lock:
            self.value += n
    def expose(self):
        return f"{self.name} {self.value}"

class Gauge:
    """Can go up or down; instantaneous state."""
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name, self.value = name, 0
        self.lock = threading.Lock()
    def set(self, v, **labels):
        with self.lock:
            self.value = v
    def expose(self):
        return f"{self.name} {self.value}"

class Histogram:
    """Buckets observations; compute p95 at query time."""
    def __init__(self, name, buckets=(5,10,25,50,100,250,500,1000,2500,5000)):
        self.name = name
        self.buckets = buckets
        self.counts = [0] * len(buckets)
        self.sum_ms = 0
        self.count = 0
        self.lock = threading.Lock()
        self.samples = []  # for percentile calc
    def observe(self, value_ms):
        with self.lock:
            for i, b in enumerate(self.buckets):
                if value_ms <= b:
                    self.counts[i] += 1
            self.sum_ms += value_ms
            self.count += 1
            self.samples.append(value_ms)
            if len(self.samples) > 10000:
                self.samples = self.samples[-10000:]
    def percentile(self, p):
        s = sorted(self.samples)
        if not s: return 0
        return s[int(len(s) * p / 100)]
    def expose(self):
        lines = [f"{self.name}_bucket{{le=\"{b}\"}} {c}"
                 for b, c in zip(self.buckets, self.counts)]
        lines.append(f"{self.name}_sum {self.sum_ms}")
        lines.append(f"{self.name}_count {self.count}")
        return "\n".join(lines)

req_total = Counter("http_requests_total")
active_conn = Gauge("active_connections")
latency = Histogram("http_request_duration_ms")

def simulate():
    for _ in range(1000):
        req_total.inc(method="GET", status="200")
        active_conn.set(random.randint(10, 200))
        latency.observe(random.expovariate(1/50))  # mean 50ms
        time.sleep(0.001)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    simulate()
    print(req_total.expose())
    print(active_conn.expose())
    print(latency.expose())
    print(f"p50={latency.percentile(50):.1f}ms p95={latency.percentile(95):.1f}ms p99={latency.percentile(99):.1f}ms")
```
